    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Tonight, YouTube brought back its film-festival-style event, Creator Premieres, to showcase a upcoming batch of “world-class, studio-quality creator programming” coming exclusively to its platform.
    • Sources indicate that last year’s Creator Premieres–the first YouTube held–took place at Upcoming York City’s historic screening space Metrograph and revealed off projects from creators like Ms.
    • This year’s edition was hosted by House Guest‘s Scott Evans at The Hollywood Roosevelt in L.A., and highlighted upcoming projects from YouTube OGs and greats like Emma Chamberlain, Nick DiGiovanni, Lilly Singh, Wesley Wang, Grace Reiter, and more.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Tonight, YouTube brought back its film-festival-style event, Creator Premieres, to showcase a upcoming batch of “world-class, studio-quality creator programming” coming exclusively to its platform.

    Sources indicate that last year’s Creator Premieres–the first YouTube held–took place at Upcoming York City’s historic screening space Metrograph and revealed off projects from creators like Ms. Rachel, Brave Wilderness, Dhar Mann, Deestroying, and Cleo Abram.

    Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

    This year’s edition was hosted by House Guest‘s Scott Evans at The Hollywood Roosevelt in L.A., and highlighted upcoming projects from YouTube OGs and greats like Emma Chamberlain, Nick DiGiovanni, Lilly Singh, Wesley Wang, Grace Reiter, and more.

    Google President Sean Downey took the stage to highlight YouTube’s continued dominance on TV screens, and gave a nod to participating creators for fueling the UGC machine that keeps viewers coming back to YouTube–on TVs and across other devices.

    Of course, he also appealed to advertisers in the same breath, reminding them that this “world-class” content is what they could be marketing alongside, if they cough up the cash to Google.

    It has been revealed that “YouTube creators are not just shaping modern culture, they are redefining the entire entertainment landscape. This slate of shows demonstrates how creators are commanding primetime attention on the significant screen and building unmatched fan loyalty,” Downey remarked. “For brands, this isn’t about buying thirty seconds of ad space; it’s about moving past standard commercial breaks and partnering directly with the storytellers who are defining modern culture.”.

    YouTube has spent years at the top of TV watch time charts–a fact that really gets under the skin of competitor Netflix. Up till recently, though, Netflix’s main response to this irritant was talking a lot of sh*t about YouTube and occasionally signing back catalog deals with view-drivers like Ms. Rachel and CoComelon.

    In a recent development, but in the last 12 months, something’s shifted. Netflix has begun tapping creators like Salish Matter, Alan Chikin Chow, and the Stokes Twins not for back catalog agreements, but for development deals–deals which result in exclusive original programming that won’t appear on YouTube.

    Industry observers note that and YouTube’s not happy about it. The platform has been offering creators money, including production financing and sweet ad deals, in exchange for turning down offers from Netflix. Conversely, creators who decide to sign with Netflix are put on YouTube’s naughty list, and denied perks like revenue shares from primo ad deals.

    It has been revealed that (That being noted, Netflix-friendly creators aren’t entirely blacklisted. DiGiovanni signed a catalog crossposting deal with Netflix in July, and was still one of the headline creators at tonight’s showcase.).

    The point we’re making here is this: With Netflix–and Disney–sniffing around, YouTube has more incentive than ever to hype up its creators and their projects on a significant stage.

    So that’s exactly what it’s doing.

After reaching billions of viewers through his global culinary adventures (@NickDiGiovanni) and step-by-step recipes (@NicksKitchen), DiGiovanni is now turning the camera solely toward fellow professional chefs, offering an unfiltered look inside kitchens around the globe. From Michelin-starred restaurants and hidden street food gems showcased in full-length episodes, to POV recipes in short-form episodes, Chef puts viewers in the shoes of the people behind the scenes, offering a unique, captivating perspective for everyone from the culinary obsessed to the simply curious. You can view the first full-length episode, “Inside the World’s #1 Pizza Restaurant” now, only on YouTube, along with the first short-form POV episode, “Butter Chicken Shawarma”. New short-form POV episodes will debut daily across Nick’s newly-debuted @Chef channel with full-length episodes rolling out throughout 2026-27 exclusively on YouTube.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that clutch is at a pivotal moment. We're growing significantly year over year, and we need more connective tissue to keep pace. We're hiring a Senior Manager, Business Operations to connect the commercial side of the house, so the teams that win, onboard, and retain our customers work from the same facts and toward the same goals. This role sits in Finance.

    This is a people manager role. You'll lead our Revenue Operations (RevOps) team and act as an operating partner to senior leaders across Sales, Marketing, Customer Success, Implementation, People, and Finance. Together with the RevOps team, you own the shared language of the business (definitions, data, and processes) so commercial teams make decisions from one view of it.

    Sources indicate that when something key doesn't have an owner yet, it lands with you: a partnership strategy, a new commercial model, or pricing and margin guidance for leadership. This is a fast-moving startup. We're building toward a much larger firm but we aren't one yet, and most of this role has no playbook. You'll define the process, build the tool, and hand it to the team. If you want established structure, this likely isn't the role.

    You'll report to the Director of Business Operations and work directly with senior leaders across the tech giant as a neutral partner to every function rather than an advocate for one. Your work will be visible, and it will significantly influence how we make commercial decisions.

    In a recent development, you'll lead a small, high-ownership RevOps team that runs the systems and data our commercial teams depend on, and creates leverage for them to do their jobs even better. The team doesn't just own systems. They build automation, tooling, and processes, and they're close partners to Sales and Marketing. You'll coach them, set priorities, and open up more strategic scope, while giving them real autonomy.

    Learn the business end to end: the revenue funnel, the customer lifecycle, how each commercial team works day to day, and where decisions get stuck.

    Build trust with your RevOps team: learn the work they own, and set priorities and team rhythms together.

    Deliver the first version of client-level margin and cost-to-serve, the analysis that grounds our pricing strategy.

    Develop a first point of view on pricing and packaging for revenue leadership, built on that analysis.

    Put AI to work in your own workflow from week one, and identify the first set of manual, repetitive processes across the commercial teams worth automating.

    Stand up a first version of a deal desk, including an approval workflow, pricing and discount guardrails, and standard commercial terms.

    Partner with Sales and Marketing leaders as they prepare for the monthly business review: pressure-test their plans and point out risks, then solve them with the RevOps team by creating newly introduced processes, tooling, or automation.

    Build on the strength of the RevOps team: prioritize its roadmap against business outcomes and take on more strategic work together.

    Launch your first AI-enabled workflows or automations that remove manual reporting or reconciliation for the commercial teams, with time saved tracked.

    Have a team whose output and standards hold, with the processes, tooling, and automation you've built running without you in the room.

    Have AI-enabled, self-serve tooling that commercial teams use day to day, with measurable time savings.

    Be the person leadership trusts to pick up the next notable thing that doesn't have an owner yet.

    5-8 years of total experience that combines consulting or banking with time as an operator inside a organization.

    Experience managing people: you've coached ICs, given direct feedback, made tough talent calls, and built team rhythms.

    According to recent reports, startup experience. You've worked in a fast-moving, ever-changing environment where structure wasn't already there, and you built it. This is not a role for someone whose experience is only at large, established enterprises.

    It has been revealed that strong analytical and financial modeling skills, including forecasting. You're very comfortable building models in spreadsheets from scratch, and they hold up to scrutiny. You use AI to move faster and sharpen your work, and you have the foundational modeling knowledge to know when its output is wrong.

    It has been revealed that data-first and self-sufficient. You open the dataset before you build the slide, you're always looking for more data to test an idea, and you're comfortable getting into raw data yourself. You use AI to analyze it faster and know enough to check its work.

    Commercial acumen: you can read commercial terms, spot the problematic ones, and reason about pricing, discounting, margin, and deal structure.

    A clear communicator who can walk an executive through a messy problem and leave them with a decision, and who is just as effective working alongside an AE, a CSM, or an engineer.

    Comfort with ambiguity. When something isn't set up yet, your instinct is to build it, not to wait for it. You create structure, manage competing priorities, and pivot when things change.

    Relentless follow-through: you close loops, and people stop checking on what you've said you'll do.

    A partner's temperament: you challenge constructively without taking sides, you surface problems early, and you resolve cross-team conflict without escalating it.

    Industry experience in fintech, financial services, lending, banking, or credit unions.

    Please note that this role may evolve as our business needs change, so we appreciate your flexibility and adaptability.

    Remote Flexibility: Enjoy the freedom of remote work from anywhere, balancing life and career seamlessly.

    Unforgettable Off-Sites: Twice a year, bond with colleagues in exciting destinations, fostering teamwork and fresh ideas.

    Paid Time Off: Enjoy flexible PTO days yearly for relaxation and rejuvenation.

    Stock Options: Joining us means having a stake in our success, so you'll receive stock options as part of your compensation package.

    Home Office Setup: Create your ideal workspace with a dedicated budget for home office essentials.

    Work Trip Budget: Grow personally and professionally with a budget for work-related trips and co-working.

    Health Coverage: Prioritize your well-being with comprehensive health and dental insurance plans.

    Sources indicate that clutch is a revolutionary vertical SaaS company, proudly backed by Andreessen Horowitz (A16z), aimed at revolutionizing the way Credit Unions engage and change the lives of their members. As a champion of financial well-being, we address the urgent need for affordable lending solutions in an era where the average American grapples with over $155,000 in household debt. Unlike traditional financial institutions, Clutch develops software to turn Credit Unions into FinTech lenders and leverage their balance sheets to responsibly lend to over 130M Americans. Our mission extends beyond mere financial transactions; we strive to fundamentally enhance the way credit unions interact with their members. By integrating cutting-edge technologies and user-centric designs, we help credit unions provide seamless digital experiences that are on par with leading tech companies. This approach not only preserves but revitalizes the longstanding tradition of community and member-focused service inherent to credit unions.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    When LIFE Magazine relaunches on November 23, one of YouTube’s biggest streamers will be front and center.

    IShowSpeed (aka Darren Watkins Jr.) has been revealed as one of five cover stars featured in LIFE ‘s relaunched debut issue, alongside fellow icons like Olympic skater Alysa Liu and actor John Malkovich.

    The issue—which describes Speed as “arguably the most famous 21-year-old on Earth”—chronicles his streaming career thus far, before looking ahead to his upcoming goals (which include livestreaming from outer space and visiting every country).

    Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

    “Nobody embodies our current moment like IShowSpeed,” Kieran Press-Reynolds, the LIFE writer who profiled Speed, remarked in his piece.

    A feature in a legacy publication isn’t exactly groundbreaking for Speed, who has been included in multiple TIME magazine lists, teamed up with brands like Expedia, gotten his own Fortnite skin, and served as the poster child for the 2026 YouTube FIFA Creator Cup.

    LIFE’s decision to feature Speed alongside an Olympic athlete and a Hollywood actor, however, is further evidence of traditional media’s growing acceptance of content creators as cultural heavyweights. Legacy publications have become increasingly eager to court creators—and woo their massive online audiences—in recent years. TIME unveiled its first-ever TIME100 Creators matter in 2025, while digital stars like MrBeast and Emma Chamberlain have served as the faces of Rolling Stone‘s own Creator Issue since 2022.

    It has been revealed that just a few days ago, Hearst Magazines rolled out Hearst Creator Studios, a division that will bring original creator content to editorial brands like Cosmopolitan, Elle, and MotorTrend. Now, as LIFE returns 90 years after its first issue, creators are taking center stage at yet another legacy magazine dedicated to covering “the stories that define our time.”.

    • The challenge for advertisers is distinguishing the passive browsers from the people with genuine purchase intent.
    • Its rental site often serves as a place for people to fantasize about their future home, even if they’re not actually looking to move.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    We’ve all been there: You look up a product out of sheer curiosity with no intent to actually spend money on it, and suddenly you’re inundated with ads for similar products.

    The challenge for advertisers is distinguishing the passive browsers from the people with genuine purchase intent.

    Zillow knows that challenge well. Its rental site often serves as a place for people to fantasize about their future home, even if they’re not actually looking to move.

    It has been revealed that “We are known for dreaming,” noted Ravi Kandikonda, SVP of marketing for Zillow Group. But that’s not necessarily a bad thing. Welcoming the dreamers is a great way for Zillow to drive awareness of its brand and get potential future renters into its platform, Kandikonda added. From there, it’s a matter of striking a balance between building awareness and driving conversions.

    That’s where Zillow turns to its media agency partner, Canvas Worldwide.

    In a recent development, in September, Canvas confirmed a new division called ART Dept., which provides a collection of AI solutions to help brands and agencies optimize their campaign budgeting and pacing. Zillow is using ART Dept.’s AI agents to better separate the renters from the dreamers and tailor its marketing accordingly.

    Sources indicate that the “ART” in ART Dept. stands for “AI Applied Research and Technology.” (Though, if we’re being pedantic, wouldn’t that be AART – or AIART?).

    Sources indicate that quibbles about acronyms aside, Canvas’ new division offers a mix of AI optimization features that are becoming commonplace for ad agencies and marketing platforms. Though, like other agentic platforms, Canvas notes its differentiation comes from how it applies those optimizations to its agentic layer.

    For example, offering a pacing dashboard is “table stakes” by now, rather than a distinguishing feature for an agency, said Sally Lee, SVP of programmatic and ART at Canvas.

    But Canvas wanted to make its pacing dashboard “multidimensional” by connecting it with a budget source of truth and building an agentic layer on top of it, said Lee.

    According to recent reports, the agentic layer, called Talos, determines whether a campaign is underpacing or overpacing and optimizes for better performance. Before pushing the newly optimized campaign into the platform, a member of the Canvas team reviews and approves (or denies) it.

    Recent findings suggest that canvas can “pick and choose from different search and behavioral categories” to optimize against, said Lee. In Zillow’s case, that might include whether a user is researching renter’s insurance or looking into moving truck rentals.

    Canvas gets those behavioral signals through its data partnerships, including its MCP connection to predictive audience targeting organization Dstillery.

    Access to behavioral data has helped Zillow reach more specific audiences and be smarter about exactly where and when to target them, said Kandikonda.

    For instance, targeting multifamily renters in Seattle using a generic, off-the-shelf “multifamily apartment buildings” audience only goes so far, he stated. “I need to know when they are on a particular platform” to bid for that audience at the right moment with the right content, he added.

    Dstillery’s audience modeling predicts which websites the target audience will visit and when based on real behavioral data. And Canvas’ AI can help surface audience and behavioral overlaps that might have previously gone overlooked by its team.

    Canvas’ reliance on data-backed reasoning was a major draw for Zillow when the two first started working together in 2023, Kandikonda remarked, and it continues to be a major focus of ART Dept.

    The goal behind the fresh product suite is to save media teams time figuring out what media is performing and how much to spend on different audience segments.

    According to recent reports, increasing ROI is key for any brand. But it’s particularly important within the real estate market, Kandikonda said, as marketing dollars are constrained and the entire industry “is bouncing around the box.”.

    So, while Zillow appreciates its dreamer audience, it’s feeling the same pressure most brands are to focus on lower-funnel conversions, such as “actual movers,” Kandikonda mentioned.

    That’s part of the reason off-the-shelf renter audiences weren’t cutting it for Zillow’s ads business, he added.

    Industry observers note that an off-the-shelf audience may indicate people who are interested in renting more broadly, he remarked, but ART was able to select for people who were actively in the process of planning a move. And more precise targeting means better lower-funnel ad performance.

    The destination, not the journey.

    From Zillow’s perspective, the biggest change from using Canvas’ ART Dept. is the results, rather than the process. After all, the AI tools are used by the Canvas team, rather than by Zillow.

    Zillow just tells Canvas what outcome it wants to achieve. Canvas then translates the desired outcome into a scorecard that weights different goals and metrics within the interoperable tech infrastructure that powers the ART Dept., which is called +Suite.

    According to recent reports, from there, Canvas’ Audience+ product (which is similar to a data management platform) connects to data partners and the Talos AI agent to build custom audiences. Finally, Talos activates and optimizes the campaign.

    The system creates an ongoing feedback loop, said Canvas’ Lee: “Build an audience, activate it, see how it’s performing against what that client cares about and identify where to make changes to drive a better outcome.”.

    Only You Can Prevent JavaScript Security Hacks; AppLovin Eyes A Criteo Acquisition

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (902 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adexchanger

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Adding to the myriad IT outages and cybersecurity scares of the past month, a major malware attack recently hit 178 publications and organizations that use Optimizely’s A/B testing and analytics tools.
    • The list included the BBC, CNN, Equifax, Ledger and Zoom, but the problem extends well beyond those high-profile sites.
    • “We’re in the age of JavaScript supply-chain attacks, and yet almost no one is talking about why content security policies were invented and how this is largely the solution for operators,” Zach Edwards, a researcher for Infoblox and the co-founder of DecryptAds, tells Daniel Krebs of Krebs on Security.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Adding to the myriad IT outages and cybersecurity scares of the past month, a major malware attack recently hit 178 publications and organizations that use Optimizely’s A/B testing and analytics tools.

    The list included the BBC, CNN, Equifax, Ledger and Zoom, but the problem extends well beyond those high-profile sites. The issue is that many operators don’t audit the tech vendors that drop JavaScript onto their pages.

    “We’re in the age of JavaScript supply-chain attacks, and yet almost no one is talking about why content security policies were invented and how this is largely the solution for operators,” Zach Edwards, a researcher for Infoblox and the co-founder of DecryptAds, tells Daniel Krebs of Krebs on Security.

    The “content security policies” (or CSPs) Edwards refers to set limits on what third-party code can do on a site, including what it can load or inject. Of the 178 affected Optimizely accounts, only 24 had CSPs in place and enforced them. Those 24 didn’t spread the malware.

    Because the malware ran in the site’s JavaScript, visitors to pages without CSPs could be infected simply by loading the page – no click or scroll required.

    In a recent development, the main offender, btw, in terms of third-party JavaScript abusers that expose sites to hackers, is ad tech, of course. It’s not even close. Which is why, unfortunately, as Krebs notes, downloading a modern ad blocker is the best solution for consumers to protect themselves.

    The rumor mill is heating up as the year winds down.

    Industry observers note that criteo has been part of that chatter for a while, with private equity firms Vista Equity and Quinti Capital reportedly interested in taking it private. Criteo hasn’t exactly thrived as a public tech giant, after all.

    But it does possess an immense graph of shopper info.

    Industry observers note that and now another contender has reportedly entered the ring. According to Reuters, AppLovin is among those in talks with Criteo.

    Big companies can use deal talks to get an inside look at the finances and operations of smaller companies. Even if the deal doesn’t happen, they’ve still gotten a peek under the hood.

    According to recent reports, amazon, for example, was rumored to have considered Criteo once upon a time – not long before launching its own off-site retargeting. Hmm.

    But Criteo would be an interesting fit for AppLovin. It plugs into a wide network of retailers and web publishers – an entirely newly introduced arena to AppLovin, which operates almost entirely in-app – and would bring a large book of business with ecommerce companies. AppLovin has remarked that it’s a priority to add advertisers to its “consumer” segment, which is primarily ecommerce.

    Criteo would offer a cheat code to get there.

    The rise of residential proxy services that hide bot traffic behind real human IP addresses has been a boon for ad fraud. Often, consumers aren’t even aware they’re acting as a proxy for bot traffic.

    Now, cheap consumer electronics with backdoor vulnerabilities built in can deliver billions of fraudulent ad impressions per day, according to a new report by HUMAN Security’s Satori Threat Intelligence and Research Team.

    In a recent development, the latest scheme Satori uncovered, which it dubbed BADBOX 3.0, was responsible for 40 billion fraudulent bid requests a day at its peak. It used the same residential proxy infrastructure as two other fraud rings that were uncovered by Satori in the past two years – hence the “3.0” branding.

    Recent findings suggest that the infrastructure relies on cheap TV sets manufactured in China by a tech giant called TXCZ. These TVs have backdoors in their operating systems that allow fraudsters to compromise them.

    Recent findings suggest that once they’re compromised, the TVs run video ads in the background that the TV owner cannot see. The bid requests for these ads use the TV owner’s IP address to appear as if they’re targeted to a real human. They also impersonate traffic from legitimate CTV apps.

    People who bought one of these TVs pretty much had no chance.

    Industry observers note that “It was compromised before you plugged it in: playing video ads you could never see and quietly renting out your home internet connection to strangers,” says HUMAN’s Gavin Reid. “Neither the advertisers paying for those ads nor the people who bought the boxes had any idea.”.

    It has been revealed that youTube adjusts its video view counts with modeled co-viewers based on its estimate of how many people saw the screen. [The Verge].

    Netflix is the frontrunner in a bidding war over the broadcast rights for the 2030 FIFA World Cup, with experts expecting FIFA to charge up to $2 billion. [The Guardian].

    Taylor Swift’s unveiled return to the Country Music Awards – her first appearance since 2013 – gave Disney and ABC a chance to squeeze more ad revenue from an event that had already sold out its inventory. [Variety].

    The former editor-in-chief of gaming industry publication Game Developer explains why she recently advised Redditors not to pursue a career in journalism and shares how multiple corporate owners failed to find viable monetization models for the publications she’s worked for since 2006. [ReaderGrev].

    Anthropic priced its initial shares at $83 apiece after demand exceeded expectations. [WSJ].

    Former Jaguar Land Rover North America CMO Charlotte Blank joins behavioral science startup Hive Science as its first-ever chief marketing officer. [MediaPost].

    #135609. Latest Update: Measuring Clicks Is Making ChatGPT Ads Look Like A Bad Bet

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (843 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Adexchanger ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: Measuring Clicks Is Making ChatGPT Ads Look Like A Bad Bet

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (843 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adexchanger

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The first question marketers ask about every latest advertising channel is almost always the same: Does it perform better than the last one we tested?
    • Sources indicate that it happened with social.
    • Industry observers note that the debate around ChatGPT advertising has rapidly become a comparison with Google Search.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The first question marketers ask about every latest advertising channel is almost always the same: Does it perform better than the last one we tested?

    Sources indicate that it happened with social. It happened with retail media. And now it’s happening with OpenAI.

    Industry observers note that the debate around ChatGPT advertising has rapidly become a comparison with Google Search. Can it deliver lower CPAs? Does it convert as well? Is it ready to compete for performance budgets?

    They’re all understandable questions. But they’re the wrong ones.

    It’s a mistake to assume conversational AI should behave like search in the first place. The customer journey is fundamentally different. If marketers continue evaluating ChatGPT using search-era metrics, there’s a real risk they’ll dismiss one of the most significant latest advertising channels before they’ve understood how it creates value.

    Google built the world’s most successful advertising business by harvesting intent.

    According to recent reports, if a user searches for “cheap hotels in Hawaii,” Google shares a list of relevant results. The commercial intent is already there. The advertiser’s job is simply to be the most relevant answer when the purchase decision is made. But conversational AI works differently.

    Instead of typing in a few keywords, a user might go into detail and explain that they’re travelling to Hawaii for a friend’s wedding, that they’re on a tight budget but want their own room, oh, and they’d like to surf while they’re there. That’s no longer a search query; it’s a conversation. And that difference matters.

    Rather than simply capturing existing demand, conversational AI helps people explore options and refine priorities before they buy. When the traveler eventually visits the website to book, they’ve often already used AI to compare all the alternatives and understand exactly what they’re looking for.

    The advertising opportunity is participating in how intent develops.

    One of the first things marketers notice when they begin testing conversational AI is that the acquisition metrics can look uncomfortable.

    Sources indicate that CPAs can appear higher than those achieved through search. For anyone used to judging performance through traditional attribution, that’s an easy reason to conclude the channel isn’t competitive.

    That was my first reaction, too.

    If it looks like search and behaves like search, surely it should produce similar economics. But once you step back and look at the customer journey rather than the click, that conclusion becomes much harder to support.

    It has been revealed that A user spending several minutes discussing products, asking follow-up questions and refining their requirements is behaving very differently from someone typing a short keyword into Google. They’re effectively qualifying themselves before they ever reach an advertiser’s website.

    That means acquisition might cost more, but the customer arriving at the other end can also be significantly better informed and a much stronger commercial fit.

    Judging conversational AI purely on CPA risks confusing efficiency with effectiveness.

    The measurement frameworks we’ve inherited aren’t suited for where the consumer journey is going.

    According to recent reports, for more than two decades, performance marketing has been built around clicks because clicks were observable. Attribution models rewarded whichever interaction happened closest to the conversion, giving marketers a practical way to optimize campaigns at scale.

    That made perfect sense in an internet dominated by search engines, display advertising and relatively linear customer journeys.

    Conversational AI changes that, because the interaction influencing a purchase often happens long before a click ever occurs. And when the eventual conversion happens later through another channel, traditional attribution naturally gives the credit elsewhere.

    That doesn’t necessarily mean the initial conversation had little value; it simply means the measurement framework wasn’t designed to capture it.

    Early evidence suggests that when marketers move beyond attribution and begin measuring incremental business outcomes instead, conversational AI looks very different from the picture painted by last-click metrics.

    According to recent reports, AI advertising can work very effectively. But unless marketers are measuring it in a way that reflects how the channel actually influences buying decisions, it can create a colossal education gap.

    The conversation today largely centers on whether OpenAI can compete with Google.

    A far better question is whether conversational AI should be evaluated like search at all.

    Every evolution in advertising has forced marketers to rethink measurement. Social wasn’t simply another display channel. Retail media wasn’t just paid search inside a retailer’s website. CTV couldn’t be judged solely through linear TV metrics.

    Conversational AI deserves the same mindset shift.

    Google monetized search intent. Conversational AI has the potential to monetize the conversation that creates it.

    Recent findings suggest that those are fundamentally different commercial models. If marketers continue measuring one using the rules of the other, they risk underestimating not only the performance of OpenAI ads, but the role conversational AI is likely to play in the future of digital advertising.

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1028 w)

    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Adexchanger ↗ Open Full Page

    Meet OpenX’s New CEO, An Optimistic Realist

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1028 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adexchanger

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Safari is cracking down on identity vendors, DSPs are going direct to publishers, Google gets to keep AdX, agents are threatening to cut out the middlemen, the walled gardens keep winning and the open web is under pressure.
    • In early November, OpenX named Robert Horler as its latest CEO, taking the reins from interim chief Joshua Metzger, who returned to his role as chief legal officer.
    • Recent findings suggest that horler joins at a time of upheaval for the ad industry and one of readjustment for OpenX.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Safari is cracking down on identity vendors, DSPs are going direct to publishers, Google gets to keep AdX, agents are threatening to cut out the middlemen, the walled gardens keep winning and the open web is under pressure.

    In early November, OpenX named Robert Horler as its latest CEO, taking the reins from interim chief Joshua Metzger, who returned to his role as chief legal officer.

    Recent findings suggest that horler joins at a time of upheaval for the ad industry and one of readjustment for OpenX. In January, the company lost John “JG” Gentry, its CEO for nearly 15 years, after a long battle with cancer.

    A 30-year veteran of agencies, advertising and ad tech, Horler previously ran Dentsu Aegis Network in the US and Northern Europe, was COO of Quantcast and, most recently, led creator agency Whalar as chief exec before it was acquired by Accenture earlier this year. He’s still on the Whalar board.

    But, given the state of the industry, how was Horler feeling roughly a week in at OpenX? Not too bad. He’s a glass-half-full kinda guy, but he’s also a pragmatist.

    “Everybody’s being disrupted,” Horler remarked. “You can pull the blanket over your head and say, ‘No thanks,’ or you can see an amazing amount of opportunity for companies that are agile and ambitious. I fancy our chances.”.

    Horler spoke with AdExchanger about Apple’s latest move, whether the sell side has the upper hand right now and the significant boots he has to fill.

    AdExchanger: Let’s start with the state of play. The assumption for a long time was that as the line blurred between the buy side and sell side, DSPs would come out on top. Now it feels like the sell side has the power. Is that how you see it?

    ROBERT HORLER: I’d agree, but it’s complicated. The pendulum has swung toward supply because advertisers want to get closer to the data and the publisher.

    Industry observers note that for the first time in about 30 years, the bigger agencies are pursuing divergent strategies for how they work with SSPs and DSPs. They all want more control, more orchestration and more influence over the revenue they drive, and I’d hypothesize that SSPs are well placed to deliver that.

    Also, no slight to The Trade Desk, but if the biggest cat in the jungle is having this many existential challenges, that tells you something’s going on.

    It has been revealed that speaking of significant cats, OpenX is suing Google, as is Magnite, PubMatic and Index Exchange. I know there’s not much you can say about OpenX’s lawsuit, if anything, but as an industry observer, what did you think of the fact that Google didn’t have to divest AdX in the federal ad tech antitrust case?

    Industry observers note that you know, it’s a shame. It’s tough for everybody who thought there would be one, but I can’t say that I’m surprised there wasn’t.

    A lot of sell-side players are going buyer-direct. So is everything just everything now? Are the distinctions between buy-side and the sell-side tech no longer meaningful?

    Industry observers note that for the people who aren’t in it, who don’t work in ad tech or programmatic advertising – and that includes some clients – the lines have always felt quite blurred. That’s not new.

    There’s probably not as much difference now as there was, though. Things are converging and overlapping and people are encroaching a bit into each other’s territories as they figure out the brave new agentic landscape. And, of course, there are also pressures that exist within their own businesses.

    But what will always be true is that publishers want to generate as much yield as possible and advertisers want to pay as little as possible, as long as it’s still effective, of course. So, yes, perhaps those lines are blurring a bit, but this natural tension will always exist.

    I know you’re still settling in, but how about you approaching Apple’s move to block identity vendors in iOS 27?

    Sources indicate that this is a major question that needs to be considered, and it’s not about workarounds; it’s about understanding it. I’m sure Joel [Meyer, OpenX’s CTO] and his team are all over it. But I don’t think it’s an existential challenge or that it represents a massively different challenge to other challenges we’ve had to navigate in the past in terms of privacy, control and all those good things.

    That’s all I can say right now other than that no one here is walking around and behaving like it’s an extinction event or something.

    Industry observers note that you spent the better part of a decade on the buy side, including as the US CEO of Dentsu. What do buyers get wrong about the sell side?

    I’d flip it, actually. The sell side needs to be simpler to partner with and more able to adapt, and sometimes they forget that. The sell side also underestimates how overwhelmed buyers are with choices.

    According to recent reports, if you show up with an overly complex sell or a raft of products that you can’t explain in simple language, you’ll just sound like everyone else. Also, don’t underestimate the importance of humanity. Trust is built around people, not just technology.

    In a recent development, I wanted to ask about John. He was such a lovely man, and his death was such a loss. How will you keep his legacy alive?

    Recent findings suggest that I never got to meet him, and I really wish I had. He was clearly beloved. When I came in for my board interview, I read the remembrance book here and it was really moving. It made me think, “If I get this job, those are big boots to fill.”.

    Recent findings suggest that the best way to honor him is to continue the mission and build a valuable company where people enjoy coming into work. John clearly believed culture is preeminent and that it’s the people who make a great company, and I want to lead with that in mind.

    This interview has been lightly edited and condensed.

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1049 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Adexchanger ↗ Open Full Page

    Don’t Give Privacy Regulators An Excuse To Come Knocking

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1049 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adexchanger

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Every time another state passes a privacy law or amends an existing one, brands have to tighten and update their vendor contracts.
    • “If you’re doing business across state borders, your data goes everywhere,” said Patrick Turner, lead counsel for data and privacy at Ford Motor Company, speaking at an event hosted by the IAB in New York City this week focused on state privacy laws.
    • And so it makes sense for contracts to always meet the strictest combination of state requirements.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Every time another state passes a privacy law or amends an existing one, brands have to tighten and update their vendor contracts.

    “If you’re doing business across state borders, your data goes everywhere,” said Patrick Turner, lead counsel for data and privacy at Ford Motor Company, speaking at an event hosted by the IAB in New York City this week focused on state privacy laws.

    And so it makes sense for contracts to always meet the strictest combination of state requirements.

    But it’s a massive chore, and everyone – colleagues, partners, ad vendors – want to know why a contract that’s worked for years suddenly needs a rewrite, Turner said. They pummel him with questions.

    “Sometimes I’ll just turn off the microphone and scream into the wall briefly,” Turner joked, “because nobody hears you when you scream in space.”.

    The latest addition to Turner’s ever-growing to-do list comes courtesy of Delaware.

    In early September, Delaware Gov. Matt Meyer signed HB 380, an amendment to the state’s privacy law that takes effect on Jan. 1, 2027, and makes due diligence mandatory.

    Under the fresh statute, companies can no longer assume a partner follows privacy laws just because it indicates so.

    It has been revealed that before sharing personal data with a third party, companies must now confirm the partner can actually meet its privacy obligations, using questionnaires and document reviews at a minimum. They also need a binding data-use contract in place. And it cuts both ways: Third parties of any size are required to cooperate with the due diligence process, and without a contract they aren’t allowed to process data at all.

    In programmatic advertising, though, vetting every partner in the supply chain would be a massive headache. A single ad campaign can bounce data between dozens of middlemen, measurement vendors and tracking pixels.

    And if every company in the chain sends every partner its own custom questionnaire, said Michael Hahn, the IAB’s SVP and general counsel, “we drown ourselves in paperwork, and nobody is any safer.”.

    But the sheer scale and complexity of ad tech doesn’t give companies a pass, said Delaware Deputy Attorney General John Eakins, who leads privacy enforcement for the state AG’s office. Sharing data through a massive programmatic network only heightens the risk to consumers, he added..

    “It requires a contract at each hop,” Eakins stated, “because each hop is a transaction involving personal data.”.

    In other words, the days of box-ticking and boilerplate are finally over.

    Paperwork isn’t compliance, said Courtney Cantor, deputy general counsel at PubMatic, who regularly fields a steady stream of due diligence requests.

    “It’s no longer about just putting the right contracts in place,” Cantor noted, “but actually having evidence to show if a regulator came knocking on your door.”.

    Although that’s assuming contracts reflect reality, which often isn’t the case.

    Take the standard clause requiring a vendor to delete everything when a customer agreement is terminated, said Gary Kibel, a partner at Davis+Gilbert. Not only do most companies not remember to do that; it’s often impossible.

    In a recent development, “I can’t delete everything” is the correct response to any deletion request, Kibel noted, because vendors have legal and record-keeping obligations of their own. On top of that, if businesses purge all of their data, they can’t do business. If you delete a client’s email address, for example, then how do you chase an unpaid bill?

    The fact is, managing retention – which Turner referred to as “the ‘R’ word” – is borderline impossible, he stated.

    Sources indicate that “Everybody puts it in their agreements; everybody says how long they’ll keep things,” Turner remarked. “But I guarantee that if I went to every single person in this room’s company and looked at your data, I’d find retention violations everywhere.”.

    Industry observers note that it’s not malicious or anything; it’s just incredibly difficult to do. “I don’t mean to inspire any attorneys general,” Turner mentioned, “but I think it’s an area we all have to be really careful about going forward.”.

    Although there’s a heck of a lot of low-hanging fruit to go after first. You’ve gotta get the basics sorted or you could be screwed.

    “I had a client about a year ago that got a letter from the Delaware attorney general’s office and they raised that problem,” he said.

    “The simple, easy things,” Turner said, “don’t let them be a problem.”.

    Recent findings suggest that and also don’t forget that regulators are also just people, he mentioned – people who read the news. When one tech giant gets sued or fined, other states take notice and start wondering whether the same thing is happening in their backyard.

    Not that getting a letter from a regulator is necessarily a DEFCON 1 situation.

    Industry observers note that these types of inquiries can feel scary because they often contain detailed questions, Kibel stated. Regulators do their homework before reaching out. But a letter isn’t a formal legal demand, and companies don’t technically have to respond.

    It’s always a good idea to engage, though, Kibel said.

    Ignoring outreach from a regulator is a surefire way to turn a voluntary back-and-forth into a subpoena.

    According to recent reports, kibel has put clients on the phone with regulators in the past, and the vibe was usually as pleasant as could be expected. “It wasn’t treated like a deposition,” he remarked, “and it wasn’t a hostile setting.”.

    Because regulators do “understand that every system is not 100% perfect,” Kibel noted.

    “But they also do want to see that you’ve thought about these problems in advance,” he said, “and that you’re being forthright with them in terms of answering their questions.”.

    Ideally, the whole thing gets worked out over a few phone calls and never escalates.

    Likewise, the purpose of Delaware’s HB 380 isn’t for the AG’s office to chase down and investigate every single third party, Eakins said. The hope is that companies and their counsel do the policing themselves.

    In a recent development, “The goal is for the industry, for you all, to be saying, ‘You know what, this counterparty is just too much of a high risk,’” Eakins stated. “I don’t trust what they’re doing with the data, so we’re just not going to take that reputational risk.”.

    GTA VI is smashing Twitch’s records—and it wants to make sure advertisers don’t miss out

    • Sources indicate that twitch isn’t taking all that buzz—or the dollar signs that come with it—for granted.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, grand Theft Auto fans across the world are still eagerly anticipating Rockstar’s long-awaited sequel to roll out in their regions. But according to data from Streams Charts, GTA VI has already smashed multiple streaming platform records—including becoming “the most popular gaming category in Twitch history by peak viewers.”.

    As of publication time, GTA VI has attracted a peak of 3.29 million concurrent viewers on Twitch, 3.19M on YouTube, and 1.5M on Kick.Those totals put it “ahead of every previous game launch tracked by Streams Charts,” the data manufacturer stated in its report.

    Sources indicate that twitch isn’t taking all that buzz—or the dollar signs that come with it—for granted. But GTA also doesn’t exactly fit into the platform’s careful approach to brand safety. So, it’s introducing new tech to ensure that advertisers can cash in on the hype surrounding GTA VI without putting their brand reputations at risk.

    Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

    Back in September, Twitch CEO Dan Clancy told hosts of The Snarketing Podcast that the platform had begun using AI to evaluate whether streamers are squeaky-clean enough for brands to run ads against their content.

    “[W]e transcribe streams to figure out ‘Is this appropriate for this brand?’” he remarked. “So that’s something that we’ve had to invest a lot in to make sure that for a brand, their content is appearing next to creators and content that fits what they’re trying to do.”.

    That update didn’t come out of nowhere: Twitch has long asked streamers to label their content in certain circumstances where mature themes or imagery are involved.

    As Gizmodo noted, this means creators have historically missed out on ad revenue when streaming mature-rated games, “because while streamers can receive donations from viewers, substantial-time monetization ultimately depends on advertising, and advertisers are generally skittish around things that might frighten the poor sensitive product-buying public.”.

    Last week, however, Clancy told Bloomberg‘s Romaine Bostick that “one of the challenges in this space is advertisers want to be part of the GTA 6 launch”—they just don’t want their ads to appear alongside the spicier parts of the game.

    To solve that problem, Twitch’s newly introduced technology will allow brands to run ads on GTA VI streams while also ensuring that (as Clancy phrased it) “any of the parts of GTA 6 that they might not want to have their ads associated with, their ads won’t be associated with that.”.

    The ins and outs of how that system will actually work remain to be seen. But if it does prove effective for GTA VI, we’ll be watching to see whether Twitch expands the tech to other streams and genres previously dismissed as unsafe for brands.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, different advertisers have different brand safety thresholds, but there are some topics that no one wants to be associated with.
    • That risk is now playing out in Spain, where several advertisers paused their TikTok ads this week.
    • Last week, Spanish news outlets reported that multiple advertisers – including Banco Santander and energy tech giant Moeve – had suspended their TikTok campaigns after ads from major Spanish brands had appeared alongside CSAM on the platform.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, different advertisers have different brand safety thresholds, but there are some topics that no one wants to be associated with. First and foremost: child sexual abuse material (CSAM).

    That risk is now playing out in Spain, where several advertisers paused their TikTok ads this week.

    Last week, Spanish news outlets reported that multiple advertisers – including Banco Santander and energy tech giant Moeve – had suspended their TikTok campaigns after ads from major Spanish brands had appeared alongside CSAM on the platform.

    Videos that either included CSAM or featured websites that sell CSAM ran before or after ads from 21 brands, Digiday reports, including Banco Santander, Samsung, Ralph Lauren and Pringles.

    TikTok has avoided taking direct responsibility in its recent statements, assuring advertisers and agencies in a note that it is “deeply committed” to ensuring that TikTok is a safe platform for teens and that it has a task force addressing the glitch.

    “We condemn child sexual abuse and exploitation,” a spokesperson tells Digiday (uh, duh), adding that it’s “categorically prohibited” on the platform.

    But, so far, these statements have done little to convince advertisers to return.

    “Until we know what’s happening, it’s better to pause,” Laura Camazón, head of digital and innovation at Mediaplus Equmedia tells Digiday. So far, three of the agency’s clients have paused their TikTok activity.

    In a week of mass technology service outages across America, Chase wants you to know that its regular service has not been disrupted.

    It has been revealed that however, one or more of Chase’s third-party tech vendors was the victim of a cyberattack. “We believe the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses,” the bank wrote in a statement on Thursday.

    In a recent development, mastercard and Visa were also tagged by a ransomware hacker org that leaked customer data. Credit card numbers were not compromised, but the data included some customer details. A Mastercard spokesperson described the leak as only touching a “limited amount of information from a subset of cardholders enrolled in a specific benefit program,” The Wall Street Journal reports.

    According to recent reports, the disclosures leave many key questions unanswered. None of the companies has named the vendors involved or specified whose data was exposed and what it included. For example, did the leaked data belong to cardholders who consented to having their data used for marketing and analytics? That would be an interesting wrinkle.

    Chase was a little more specific about next steps, though, at least.

    “Where appropriate, we will contact affected customers directly and offer support, including complimentary credit monitoring,” it mentioned in its response.

    On Thursday, Anthropic IPO’d at a cool $2 trillion, making it the first of the leading AI companies to go public.

    Its share price opened at $111.50, then dropped to roughly $100 within its first hour on the market.

    The timing is striking. Anthropic’s public launch comes just a week after ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang stepped down from his role at the firm, following a leaked affair with a woman rumored to be a Chinese spy.

    Industry observers note that huang’s departure left a gaping hole in AI funding. The industry may miss him for other reasons, too, but the bigger concern is capital.

    Industry observers note that “Nvidia is carrying almost every AI-native startup from application to neocloud,” Shamillah Bankiya, a partner at Dawn Capital, tells TechCrunch. Colette Kress, Huang’s temporary replacement as Nvidia’s CEO, is expected to be “much more conservative,” another investor adds.

    Still, Anthropic’s blockbuster IPO goes to show that the AI bubble isn’t at risk of popping quite yet.

    But it certainly “contrasts with an anxious moment for investors,” The Latest York Times writes, amid growing concerns over AI regulation and public backlash against the technology.

    According to recent reports, influencers claim creators can earn up to $5,000 by clipping Grand Theft Auto VI gameplay videos that hit a million views. In reality, YouTube Shorts typically pays just $30 to $100 per million views. [Benzinga].

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (742 w)

    Breaking: Q3 In Review: Pay TV Shrinks, Streaming And Sports Step Up

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (742 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adexchanger

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Have you been keeping up with the quarterly earnings scoreboard for media and entertainment companies?
    • Industry observers note that it’s a lot, we know.
    • Before you hunker down for Turkey Day, here’s a rundown on the TV and streaming companies (those that remain after all the recent consolidation, that is) that posted their earnings for the three months ending on Sept.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Have you been keeping up with the quarterly earnings scoreboard for media and entertainment companies?

    Industry observers note that it’s a lot, we know. Not to worry. We figured you’d be busy, and so we tuned in to Q3 call after Q3 call so you didn’t have to. (You’re welcome.).

    Before you hunker down for Turkey Day, here’s a rundown on the TV and streaming companies (those that remain after all the recent consolidation, that is) that posted their earnings for the three months ending on Sept. 30 – and what these reports reveal about the state of TV and media today.

    Netflix’s Q3 numbers look decent on paper. Revenue rose 12% year over year to $12.9 billion, while advertising revenue alone has spiked over 80% this year. But Netflix wasn’t able to double its ad revenue again this year as planned. To be fair, growing ad revenue promptly was easier to do back when Netflix first started its ads biz from scratch.

    On the advertising front, Netflix also touted improved programmatic targeting and ad measurement capabilities, including a pixel to measure conversions.

    Industry observers note that comcast’s media division reported $5.4 billion in earnings last quarter, a 13% YOY jump from this time last year. Alongside NBCUniversal, which Comcast prepares to spin off as a standalone firm alongside British broadcaster Sky, Comcast’s media division also includes NBCU’s Peacock, Telemundo, Bravo and Universal film and television studios.

    But Comcast had weaker performance across the broadband and theme park sides of the business, which saw a 6.1% revenue decline. (The theme parks live under the Universal brand and will go with NBCU and Sky in the spin-off.).

    According to recent reports, unlike Netflix, Fox boasted of recent boosts in engagement. Its free ad-supported TV platform, Tubi, saw a 23% YOY increase in viewing hours, thanks in part to the platform’s recent focus on creator content.

    According to recent reports, zooming out from Tubi, Fox’s overall revenue rose 22% to $4.6 billion last quarter, including a 47% jump in advertising revenue. But, sports and streaming aside, it wasn’t all sunshine and rainbows. Fox News saw major viewership declines throughout the year and into October, when total-day ratings fell 27% ahead of the midterms.

    Fox was vague about details regarding its acquisition of Roku but asserted it expects to close the deal soon. A mere few days later, on Nov. 6, Fox revealed it officially completed the acquisition.

    Versant Media, which spun off from Comcast in January, posted a 4% decline in Q3 revenue, a loss it mostly blamed on secular declines in the pay-TV industry.

    Versant also closed its acquisition of Full Swing last quarter, a deal that supports its ambitions to lean on live sports – golf in particular – as a competitive advantage.

    Skydance closed its acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery on Oct. 4, so there were no WBD-specific numbers in its Q3 report. But WBD aside, Skydance reported $7 billion in revenue last quarter, representing 5% YOY growth.

    Streaming was a highlight, with Paramount+ revenue jumping 21% YOY to just over $2.1 billion. Skydance also announced plans to launch a service combining HBO Max and Paramount+ at the beginning of next year.

    Skydance CEO David Ellison confirmed that Paramount+ and Pluto are officially operating on the same ad tech stack, noting that integrating HBO Max should be a relatively speedy process.

    Disney reported a 16% revenue jump to $25.9 billion in Q4 (its fiscal year ends in September) and a revenue increase of 8% to $102.3 billion for the full year.

    In a recent development, ad revenue grew 10% to $1.7 billion within Disney’s entertainment segment. For its sports segment, that growth rate was 20%.

    Disney also shared that it’s unifying Disney+ and Hulu into one app beginning next month. The company will add more sports to Disney+ in December and introduce creator content from TikTok into the Disney+ mobile app.

    Sports streamer Fubo, which also ends its fiscal year in September, saw its fourth-quarter revenue inch up to $1.5 billion from $1.48 billion during the same period last year.

    In a recent development, but Fubo suffered a net loss of $51.8 million in its Q4 – a heavier loss than the $38.8 million it posted in the same quarter last year. Fubo attributed the loss to operational and restructuring costs related to its recent merger with Hulu + Live TV.

    Thanks for reading and happy streaming!

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Disney continues to prove that Netflix isn’t the only competitor sniffing around YouTube‘s top talent.
    • According to recent reports, for their deal, 36-year-old L.A.-based King will make 10 original short-form videos, which Disney will have exclusive rights to distribute.
    • One of the King projects coming to Disney+ is Cardboard Wars, his 52-minute intentionally-low-budget tribute to Star Wars: A New Hope.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Disney continues to prove that Netflix isn’t the only competitor sniffing around YouTube‘s top talent.

    According to recent reports, for their deal, 36-year-old L.A.-based King will make 10 original short-form videos, which Disney will have exclusive rights to distribute. Disney indicates the agreement “will also bring [King’s] signature illusions to upcoming content for Disney+ and [King’s] own channels inspired by Disney’s Hexed, Star Wars, and other Disney films and experiences.”.

    Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

    One of the King projects coming to Disney+ is Cardboard Wars, his 52-minute intentionally-low-budget tribute to Star Wars: A New Hope. King uploaded the film to YouTube in August, and soon will cross-post it to Disney’s streaming service.

    A post shared by Zach King (@zachking).

    But there’s still more: King will pop up on Disney’s social accounts as well, hosting behind-the-scenes content about the VFX and filmmaking techniques he uses in his content.

    According to recent reports, “I fell in love with filmmaking and storytelling as a young kid, grabbing my parents’ home video camera and teaching myself to edit,” King wrote in an Instagram post. “A lot of my early homemade films were inspired by the Disney movies and the behind-the-scenes footage they would show in the DVD featurettes. There was always a sense of magic I would see on the screen, and so I’m thrilled to be working with Disney to continue that magic of filmmaking for the next generation of storytellers.”.

    It has been revealed that king has worked with Disney regularly in recent months: He was at its glitzy Created in L.A. event in September, and earlier this month played a game of viral format Cake or Fake? with Hexed (and Arcane, and Sinners, and Spider-Verse, and Hawkeye) star Hailee Steinfeld. But this is his first official, expansive content deal.

    “Zach makes the impossible look real, bringing the kind of imagination and originality that has always defined Disney,” Asad Ayaz, The Walt Disney Company’s CMO and Brand Officer, noted in a statement. “He brings both a filmmaker’s ingenuity and a fan’s passion to our stories, along with a unique connection with audiences. We want to build lasting relationships with creators like Zach, giving their ideas room to grow across Disney. That’s what makes this next chapter of our work together so full of possibility.”.

    As we mentioned above, everyone–including YouTube–has had their eye on Netflix’s obvious poaching efforts…leaving room for Disney to sneak in the back.

    In a recent development, in the last couple months, Disney has unveiled deals with major creators Dhar Mann, Dude Perfect, and Like Nastya. Crucially, these are all development deals–the exact kind of agreement that has YouTube on guard with Netflix.

    According to recent reports, and Disney’s not quite showing its full hand just yet. During its earnings call Nov. 17, executives only mentioned YouTubers once, in passing and in reference to Disney+’s growing crop of approved creator content.

    We suspect more is in the pipeline–and that YouTube may have to start paying creators to turn down Disney deals, too.

    Our customers trust us with audio, video and data belonging to their own end consumers, so a security failure on our side puts their data and their business at risk. We are hiring a Security Engineer to build and run our vulnerability management and security operations program. Vulnerability management is a core capability for keeping our security posture strong as the platform and the organization grow: knowing what we run, finding what is exposed, and getting the right fixes shipped quickly.     Experience supporting compliance audits such as HIPAA, PCI-DSS, ISO 27001 or SOC 2.

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (694 w)
    📖 Baca
    General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Adexchanger ↗ Open Full Page

    Ampersand Is Offloading Its Indie Agency Business To Comcast And Spectrum Following Mass Layoffs

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (694 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adexchanger

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Bridging the gap between linear TV and streaming is apparently easier said than done.
    • Ampersand, a TV ad platform that combines linear and streaming data from national and local markets to unify audience targeting and measurement, is significantly paring back its business, AdExchanger has learned.
    • The company, a joint venture established in 2019 by Comcast, Charter and Cox (which Charter now owns), will offload its independent agency business to Comcast Advertising and Charter’s Spectrum Reach in 2027.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Bridging the gap between linear TV and streaming is apparently easier said than done.

    Ampersand, a TV ad platform that combines linear and streaming data from national and local markets to unify audience targeting and measurement, is significantly paring back its business, AdExchanger has learned.

    The company, a joint venture established in 2019 by Comcast, Charter and Cox (which Charter now owns), will offload its independent agency business to Comcast Advertising and Charter’s Spectrum Reach in 2027.

    Recent findings suggest that in October, Ampersand sent a memo to clients announcing the decision effective Jan. 1, an Ampersand spokesperson confirmed.

    Ampersand will continue operating, but with a focus on agency holding companies and political advertising.

    The decision comes on the heels of recent layoffs at Ampersand.

    According to recent reports, ampersand didn’t share more details with AdExchanger about the rationale behind its decision to hand off indie agency ad sales. But the client memo, which AdExchanger viewed, reveals some hints.

    Per the memo: “This new model will give independent agencies more direct access to Comcast Advertising and Spectrum Reach’s differentiated capabilities across premium video, streaming, data and technology, advanced audiences, measurement and attribution.”.

    To be fair, media buyers are increasingly seeking more direct access to TV and streaming inventory as they prioritize cost-cutting and ad performance. Indie agencies, it seems, would rather bypass Ampersand as their go-between and tap Comcast or Spectrum directly instead.

    The memo also suggests that indie agencies may value certain capabilities that are unique to Comcast and Spectrum’s ad tech stacks.

    In a recent development, additionally, Ampersand specializes in local TV advertising. So, perhaps indie agencies are less interested in direct access to local TV inventory these days than, say, political advertisers are.

    Meanwhile, Ampersand has been struggling lately, at least judging by recent rounds of layoffs, which the company did not publicly announce.

    There were several significant layoffs over the past year and change, a source with knowledge of Ampersand’s business told AdExchanger anonymously.

    Glassdoor reviews also indicate a bleak state of affairs, along with rumors of the company’s full shutdown. “There have been mass layoffs over the past two years,” a former Ampersand account executive wrote in October. “Most people expect the company to close in the next 2-3 years.”.

    AdExchanger first reached out to Ampersand after hearing rumors of a full shutdown from a source familiar with the company, but Ampersand denied these rumors and emphasized that it will continue to operate next year.

    Other Glassdoor reviews, however, are similarly pessimistic about the company’s long-term viability.

    According to recent reports, the current leadership is “driving the company into extinction,” another account executive wrote in October while still employed at Ampersand. “Over the last few years, they have done little to develop or improve products or relationships. Instead, they have focused on reducing staff.”.

    Ampersand confirmed to AdExchanger that the decision to offload its indie agency business to Comcast and Spectrum have impacted roles, but declined to share specifics. Ampersand also acknowledged an unrelated round of layoffs in 2024.

    Recent findings suggest that the future remains uncertain, but what’s clear is Ampersand’s ambitions to focus on reliable sources of TV ad demand: holdcos and political advertising. (And streaming, of course, because, well, duh.).

    In January, Ampersand launched a fresh ad platform called TrueStream Political, aiming to help political advertisers more accurately reach voters across connected TV environments. Part of the platform’s pitch is its ability to reconcile audience and identity across disparate CTV platforms, a persistent challenge for CTV media buyers.

    It makes sense for Ampersand to focus more on political ad buying. Political advertisers spent $12.06 billion leading up to the 2026 midterm elections, according to AdImpact, marking the first time a midterm cycle topped a presidential election in terms of ad spend.

    But although political advertising has seen a recent uptick during non-election years, it still tends to be very seasonal. You can, however, bank on a major influx of political ad dollars coming in roughly every two years.

    So, sure, streaming and political are hot right now. But will this sharpened focus help Ampersand survive into the future? Well … stay tuned.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Snap’s Head of Performance Marketing GTM Rick Lucas and Kitsch CMO Ying Ying Kuang on why relying on last-click attribution hides your best customers, and how Clicks + Deterministic Views (CDV) paint a fuller picture of conversion.

    Consumer behavior is changing, and marketers hunting for incremental growth need to look beyond traditional discovery.

    As audiences turn to DMs and group chats to make purchase decisions, standard last-click platform reports miss authentic peer recommendations.

    In this episode of Inside the Stack, Snap’s Head of Performance Marketing GTM, Rick Lucas, and Kitsch CMO Ying Ying Kuang explain why last-click attribution—while still essential—isn’t the whole story.

    They discuss how Kitsch used a 16% geo-lift holdout test to prove Snap’s incremental value beyond the click, why Clicks + Deterministic Views (CDV) are necessary to capture real demand, and how to get comfortable living in the “messy middle” of continuous testing.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that OK, so Netflix failed to buy Warner Bros.
    • That potential acquisition is apparently top of wishlist for Netflix (and Variety already deemed it “Hollywood’s Next Substantial Deal”), but Comcast co-CEOs Mike Cavanagh and Brian Roberts say they’re not selling.
    • Well, according to Bloomberg, the current plan is for Netflix to revamp its approach to permanent interactive IRL installations, aka Netflix Houses.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that OK, so Netflix failed to buy Warner Bros. Discovery.

    What if it bought NBCUniversal, tho?

    That potential acquisition is apparently top of wishlist for Netflix (and Variety already deemed it “Hollywood’s Next Substantial Deal”), but Comcast co-CEOs Mike Cavanagh and Brian Roberts say they’re not selling.

    Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

    Well, according to Bloomberg, the current plan is for Netflix to revamp its approach to permanent interactive IRL installations, aka Netflix Houses. The streamer first unveiled these in 2023, with a demo setup that looked like someone stocked the gift shop in Jurassic Park with merch of the laser murder doll from Squid Game.

    At the time, Josh Simon, Netflix’s then-VP of Consumer Products (now CEO of collectibles company Funko) said the concept for Netflix Houses came from knowing “fans love to immerse themselves in the world of our movies and TV shows,” and “thinking a lot about how we take that to the next level.”.

    Sources indicate that netflix had flirted with pop-ups before that; those were mainly focused on selling stuff. Make no mistake, Netflix Houses are also focused on selling stuff, but in a Disney World kind of way, where fans pay $39 to enter the House and head through an art gallery-esque space filled with themed exhibits like exclusive theater demonstrates, movie/TV set recreations, VR experiences, and arcade games. There are cafeterias and merch shops, but by and large the things to buy share billing with things to do.

    The Houses are permanent installations (for now just in Dallas and Philly, with one planned to open in Vegas in 2027) but the exhibits within rotate regularly to keep up with whatever’s trending on Netflix.

    This year, for example, the Houses were renovated to feature animated smash megahit KPop Demon Hunters. They’ve also spotlighted Stranger Things, One Piece, Wednesday, and the aforementioned Squid Game.

    Per Bloomberg, Netflix initially planned to open dozens of Houses across the U.S., focusing on quieter suburban areas away from downtowns. It wanted to snap up spaces in malls, which are not doing very well and might be willing to rent for cheap.

    But apparently the results from its first two Houses haven’t been quite what Neflix expected, so it’s pausing openings beyond Vegas until it can reassess.

    Sources indicate that people familiar with the matter told Bloomberg the Philadelphia location has daytime draws like mini golf and a movie theater, but doesn’t see much traffic at night. Dallas, meanwhile, is breaking even financially, and has done well with larger groups and corporate events.

    Netflix is also planning to see what comes from its Las Vegas location. Vegas, as you may know, is not in fact a quieter suburban locale–so if the House there proves to be profitable, with more traffic than Dallas and Philly, Netflix could reconsider where it opens in the future.

    Sources indicate that people familiar with the matter said Netflix is also looking at maybe taking Houses overseas. But wherever the next one ends up, it probably won’t open for at least another year, they said, until significant data from all three flagship U.S. locations is in.

    In a recent development, now, with all this in mind, it’s worth remembering Netflix just shock-fired its longtime Chief Content Officer Bela Bajaria and replaced her with Peter Rice, Disney‘s former General Entertainment Chairman. Film chief Dan Lin is out too. Clearly, Netflix hopes to revamp more than its IRL installations…and perhaps it’s hoping Rice’s Disney EXP comes in handy with the Houses?

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Four and a half years after winning a Grammy for The Unofficial Bridgerton Musical, the songwriting duo known as Barlow & Bear has something fresh in store for TikTok viewers.

    Sources indicate that abigail Barlow and Emily Bear are two of the creators behind To Die For Love, an 81-episode musical microdrama co-produced by TikTok and Ampersand. According to TikTok, the series follows “an ambitious half-witch vying for her coven’s crown. When she falls for a mortal, their romance takes an unexpected turn, forcing an impossible choice between family and the love of her life.”.

    Barlow & Bear created an original score for To Die For Love, while Barlow co-wrote the script alongside Oscar-nominated writer/director, actor, and opera singer Julia Aks.

    Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

    Barlow also stars in the series opposite Broadway vet Derek Klena. Executive producers include Ampersand CEO Agnes Chu, Benj Pasek, Justin Paul, Danielle Perelman, Chris Crema, Matthew Ko, and Kevin Weaver.

    “Making To Die For Love has been one of the most rewarding creative experiences of our careers,” Barlow and Bear remarked. “We love a pressure cooker, and building an entire musical in under five months proved that meaningful storytelling isn’t about time—it’s about the story and the people bringing it to life.”.

    This isn’t the first creator-driven microdrama TikTok has brought to life. Earlier this year, Issa Rae’s media company, HOORAE, struck a deal with the platform to produce short-form web series for both TikTok and its companion app PineDrama. The first vertical series to emerge from that partnership, Screen Time, had racked up over 620 million views on TikTok and PineDrama as of late October, making it both platforms’ most-viewed show to date.

    TikTok doubled down on that success last month when it unveiled a new microseries-focused partnership with Made By Us Studios, which describes itself as a “first-of-its-kind, Hollywood-grade studio designed for the creator economy and powered by creator management organization MADE BY ALL.”.

    In a recent development, now, TikTok is forging ahead into the world of musical microdramas. To Die For Love will be available exclusively on TikTok and PineDrama, with all 81 episodes premiering December 21. The original soundtrack will be released by Atlantic Records.
